newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parties agree on Finance Ministry reform.
newsitem.headline: Japan parties agree on Finance Ministry reform.

text.p: The three parties in Japan's loose ruling alliance agreed on Tuesday on a plan to reform the powerful Finance Ministry and strip it of its role of inspecting and supervising financial institutions.
But the plan, the subject of intense debate between the parties in recent weeks, may still leave the ministry with a good deal of authority over dealing with financial crises.
"We have reached a basic agreement... We will report to the prime minister," a senior party official said. He did not disclose details of the agreement.

Government officials have said that bills to implement the reform plan will be drafted by the cabinet's legislation bureau and submitted to the next regular session of parliament, which meets in late January. The reforms are expected to be implemented during the fiscal year starting in April 1998.

The ministry, long viewed as the pinnacle of Japan's elite bureaucracy, has come under fire for its handling of the nation's banking woes, including the secretive manner in which it deals with crises.
Reform of the ministry is also seen as the first step in Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's plan to carry out a broad streamlining of central government agencies by 2001.

Japanese media reported that the final plan calls for a fully independent body under the Prime Minister's Office to oversee all financial institutions -- banks, agricultural financial firms, non-bank financial firms and labour credit associations -- which are are now supervised by different ministries.
Other ministries such as agriculture and trade would also play a role in overseeing the firms, the reports said.

The Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), which forms a minority government, has been at odds with the two small parties which support it in a loose alliance, the Social Democrats and the Sakigake Party, over details of the reforms.
Differences emerged over how much independence the new body should be given and what role it should play in financial crises.

Under Tuesday's agreement, the head of the new body, tentatively named the Financial Inspection and Supervision Agency, would be appointed by the prime minister and would have the right to appoint agency employees.
It stopped short of clearly banning personnel exchanges between the agency and the ministry, media reports said.
The three-party accord also called for regular meetings between the new agency and the ministry to maintain stablility in the financial system.

The new agency would be responsible for handling financial failures but would be expected to consult with the finance minister on any failures that could not be handled within the current framework of procedures. Severe crises would be dealt with at the cabinet level, media reports said.
The Finance Ministry will still establish policies for supervising the financial industry, but the accord stressed the need to separate fiscal policy and financial policy completely by 2001.
The ministry's regional bureaux would also retain a role in the inspection and supervision of regional financial institutions.
The parties agreed that the new agency would have jurisdiction over Japan's Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), the media reports said.
The parties also agreed that the ministry's banking and securities bureaux should merge and take over some of the functions of the international finance bureau.
